title: Record Cyclosporiasis Outbreak Exposes Gaps Left by Federal Health Surveillance Cuts
excerpt: With nearly 16,000 confirmed cases across 47 states, former CDC and FDA officials say Trump-era funding cuts have slowed the response to the worst parasitic food outbreak in U.S. history.
body:
• The CDC has reported 15,716 confirmed cyclosporiasis cases across 47 states as of August 17, with 828 hospitalizations and two deaths — seven times the previous record.
  • An additional 11,841 suspected cases are under investigation, and the outbreak has been linked to recalled iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico.
  • Former FDA and CDC officials say federal health surveillance cuts, including the removal of Cyclospora from the FoodNet monitoring program and staff reductions at food safety agencies, have hobbled the government's response.
  • A food traceability rule from 2011 that could have helped contain the outbreak was delayed again earlier this year.

The numbers are staggering. As of August 17, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 15,716 cases of cyclosporiasis across 47 states — seven times the previous U.S. record for the parasitic infection. At least 11,841 additional suspected cases remain under investigation. Two people have died, and 828 have been hospitalized.

The outbreak, the largest foodborne illness event in recent American history, has been linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, which prompted a nationwide recall in July. But as the case count continues to climb, former federal health officials are raising pointed questions about whether the U.S. government's response has been hampered by its own decisions.

A Gutted Surveillance System

Last year, the CDC scaled back its Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network — known as FoodNet — removing six of eight pathogens from its core monitoring list. Cyclospora, the parasite responsible for cyclosporiasis, was among them.

J. Glenn Morris Jr., who helped establish FoodNet in 1995 during his time at the USDA, told Healio that the cuts meant investigators entered this outbreak with less baseline information than in any prior crisis.

"Without FoodNet, it meant that going into the outbreak, the people who were investigating it had less information."

— J. Glenn Morris Jr., founding contributor to FoodNet

Dan Jernigan, who oversaw the CDC's infectious disease unit until resigning last summer, told NPR that with funding and staff down roughly 50%, his former colleagues are triaging — working only on outbreaks that span multiple states rather than assisting states on every Cyclospora case, as they had done historically.

FDA's International Team Disbanded

Susan Mayne, who ran the FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition until three years ago, told NPR that the branch once employed 1,100 people plus a cadre of inspectors. The Trump administration's sweeping cuts eliminated teams that coordinated outbreak response with counterparts in other countries — a critical function when the contamination source is Mexican-grown lettuce.

"They were all let go. And now we have this outbreak with Mexico. I don't know who's managing that partnership. Those relationships obviously have been disrupted."

— Susan Mayne, former head of FDA Center for Food Safety

A Health and Human Services spokesperson told NPR that the foreign liaison team has since been reinstated. But Mayne pointed to another casualty: microbiologists and epidemiologists in federally funded labs who conducted research on Cyclospora. Much of that lab funding came through USAID, the international aid agency the Trump administration shuttered.

Michigan Bears the Brunt

Michigan, the hardest-hit state, has reported 13,909 cases. State officials said last week that the rise in numbers largely reflected a processing backlog rather than a continued acceleration, suggesting the worst may be over. But the CDC is investigating at least six additional clusters beyond the main lettuce-linked outbreak, for which sources have not yet been confirmed.

Only three states — Delaware, Hawaii, and Montana — have been spared entirely.

A Delayed Traceability Rule

Mayne also highlighted a food traceability rule, originally developed in 2011, that was delayed again earlier this year. The rule would require barcodes on produce capable of tracking contamination to its source within 24 hours.

Without it, investigators must rely on slower interview-based methods to trace the path of contaminated produce through the supply chain — a process that can take weeks for a pathogen like Cyclospora, whose symptoms often do not appear for a week or more after exposure.

What Consumers Should Do

Cyclosporiasis is caused by consuming food or water contaminated with the Cyclospora parasite. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, cramping, bloating, and nausea that can persist for weeks without treatment. The standard treatment is a course of the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

The outbreak has rattled consumer confidence in fresh produce nationwide. The CDC has said it continues to work with state health departments, the FDA, and the USDA to investigate the ongoing clusters. For now, the recalled Taylor Farms lettuce has been removed from the supply chain, but the broader question remains: whether the surveillance infrastructure will be rebuilt before the next outbreak arrives.
